Article Title: ICMR hands over homegrown cervical pre-cancer treatment, vaccine technologies to pharma firms
Article Text:
ICMR transfers medical technologies under Patent Mitra Initiative

NEW DELHI: A potential new treatment for cervical pre-cancer and two next-generation vaccines against typhoid and other gut infections have moved a step closer to becoming available in India after the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) licensed the technologies to Indian pharmaceutical companies. If successful, the indigenous products could improve access to affordable treatment and vaccines while reducing dependence on imported technologies.The technologies have been transferred under ICMR’s Medical Innovations Patent Mitra initiative, which helps convert government-funded research into products that can be developed, tested and eventually brought to the market.Among them is SHetA2, a potential treatment for Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia (CIN), a precancerous condition caused by persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). If left untreated, CIN can progress to cervical cancer, one of the leading cancers among Indian women.Unlike surgery, which is commonly used to remove abnormal cells, SHetA2 is designed to selectively destroy HPV-infected abnormal cells while sparing healthy cells. Scientists believe it could offer women a safer and less invasive treatment option in the future. The technology has been licensed to Emcure Pharmaceuticals for further development, clinical testing and commercialisation.ICMR has also licensed two vaccine technologies developed by its National Institute for Research in Bacterial Infections (NIRBI), Kolkata, to Biological E. One is a next-generation vaccine against typhoid, while the other is designed to protect against typhoid, paratyphoid and Shigella, bacteria that cause severe diarrhoea and other intestinal infections, particularly among children.The vaccine candidates will now undergo further development and evaluation before they can be considered for regulatory approval and public use.Dr Rajiv Bahl, Secretary, Department of Health Research, and Director General, ICMR, said partnerships between researchers and industry are helping move promising discoveries from laboratories to patients while strengthening India’s biomedical innovation ecosystem.The technology transfer is part of ICMR’s broader effort to support indigenous healthcare innovation through patent protection, technology licensing, clinical validation and regulatory facilitation, with the aim of making affordable medicines and vaccines available to patients.
Article Summary: The technologies have been transferred under ICMR’s Medical Innovations Patent Mitra initiative. If successful, the indigenous products could improve access to affordable treatment and vaccines while reducing dependence on imported technologies. Among them is a potential treatment for Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia (CIN)

Article Title: Florida scientists used female Burmese pythons as live lures to find invasive males in the Everglades, but 3 million camera-trap photos produced only four python detections
Article Text:
Conservancy biologists with a 16ft, 135lb female Burmese python found while radio-tracking a male scout snake in southwest Florida in February 2025.

Southeastern Naturalist

Captivity stress and chemical signals

The ongoing battle in the Everglades

Removal programs and public support

Florida scientists used female Burmese pythons as live lures to find invasive males in the Everglades, but 3 million camera-trap photos produced only four python detections.A study published in the journalshows that placing wild-caught female Burmese pythons (Python bivittatus) in cages across the Greater Everglades Ecosystem failed to draw in wild males.Over a 90-day field test at 12 locations, researchers filtered more than three million camera-trap photos using artificial intelligence software. They recorded just three python visits at the cages holding female lures and one visit at empty control cages.The study, titled "Not so fatal attraction: Captive female Burmese Python lures do not improve wild python detection," was written by Alex D. Potash, Maggie Jones, Michael Kirkland, Jenna Cole, Kristen Hart, and Robert A. McCleery. The research record was published by the USGS Publications Warehouse and carried out through the USGS Wetland and Aquatic Research Center.In controlled laboratory settings, male pythons show a strong interest in the scents given off by breeding females. However, the scientists suggest that the stress of living in cages may have stopped the captive females from releasing pheromones, removing the chemical scent needed to attract wild males.Understanding how pythons communicate is still limited. The authors note that finding better care methods to reduce stress in captured females could improve future tests, while further work on python chemistry might help create fake scents to track the invasive snakes.The failed female lure test follows another setback with scent tracking. In an August 2025 study published in Management of Biological Invasions, titled "Mammalian scent lures fail to increase detections of invasive Burmese pythons (Python bivittatus)," researchers tested whether rabbit scent could replace live prey.Written by Storm Miller, Michael Kirkland, Kristen Hart, and Robert A. McCleery of the USGS Wetland and Aquatic Research Center, the 84-day experiment across 21 sites brought only 11 python sightings. Four pythons were seen near rabbit scent lures (poop, urine, and hair) and seven near plain soil. While the rabbit scent attracted more native snakes by drawing in live mice and rats, it did not draw in pythons.These scent experiments show how hard it is to find a top predator that has wiped out native mammals like marsh rabbits, foxes, raccoons, and deer.Pythons spread through South Florida in the 1990s when escaped or released pets entered the wild. Today, tens of thousands live in the wetlands. Females can lay up to 100 eggs a year, making control efforts urgent.Despite scent lure challenges, state teams and conservation groups report steady progress through hunting and radio tracking.The Conservancy of Southwest Florida recently announced it has removed 20 tons of pythons from the wild over a decade, setting a single-season record by taking 6,300 pounds of snakes out of a 200-square-mile area since November.The conservancy's main strategy relies on fitting wild male "scout" snakes with radio trackers during the November-to-April breeding season. The tagged males lead biologists straight to breeding groups, allowing teams to catch large females before they lay eggs.“There’s very good evidence that the scout snake program is our most effective and least biased method. It doesn’t just limit us to targeting human accessible areas and it’s super targeted toward those reproductive females,” said Andrew Durso, a herpetologist at Florida Gulf Coast University. “But it’s expensive to radio-track these males into remote parts of the Everglades where you can’t go very easily. You need air support from a helicopter, which ups the price per python removed. It’s all a balance sheet of how do we want to spend money?”Ian Bartoszek, science project manager and chief wildlife scientist at the Conservancy of Southwest Florida, noted that his team's work has stopped roughly 20,000 eggs from hatching since 2013.“Through years of research we’ve developed science-based methods to track this apex predator more effectively and mitigate its damage to our native wildlife population,” said Bartoszek. “Burmese pythons are impressive creatures that are here from no fault of their own. As wildlife biologists, we have tremendous respect for all snake species. However, we understand the impact invasive pythons are having on the biodiversity in our area and we humanely remove them from the ecosystem. ”The South Florida Water Management District has separately tracked and removed over 15,650 pythons through its Python Elimination Program, which hires paid snake hunters. Public support stays high, aided by annual events like the Florida Python Challenge, which drew 895 hunters who caught 195 pythons in 2024.Mike Kirkland, python program manager at the district, sees signs that removal work is helping key areas.“Every single python that’s removed is positive for the environment,” said Kirkland. “We’re getting better and better at removing this invasive species. We’re learning more about their behavior and life history, and their non-native range here in south Florida, which is leading to more removals and hopefully innovation and novel strategies going forward.”Kirkland added that removing every single python across the wetlands may not be possible, but local populations are changing.“Progress is being made. Anecdotally we’re seeing some demographic shifts, and regionally, we’re seeing less larger size-class pythons in certain areas. That’s a direct result of our management efforts, and our partners’ management efforts,” Kirkland said.“As with most environmental issues, a multi-pronged strategy of different efforts working in concert with one another is really the best path forward,” Kirkland added. “In the future I see the python population being greatly reduced, and to a point where we can begin to see a robust return of our native animal populations, which is why we’re doing all this to begin with. I’m confident we’re going to be able to manage this species to the point where we’re seeing our deer populations, our foxes, our possums, our raccoons and so on, restored to the Everglades. ”Burmese pythons (Python bivittatus) are among the world's largest snakes, commonly growing 10–16 feet (3–5 metres) long, with some exceeding 18 feet (5.5 metres). Native to Southeast Asia, they are non-venomous constrictors that kill prey by cutting off blood flow before swallowing it whole using flexible jaws. They can eat animals as large as deer and alligators, then survive for weeks or even months without another meal. Females may lay more than 100 eggs in one clutch and protect them until they hatch. In Florida's Everglades, where they are invasive, Burmese pythons have caused major declines in several native mammal populations.
Article Summary: Florida scientists used female Burmese pythons as live lures to find invasive males in the Everglades, but 3 million camera-trap photos produced only four python detections. The stress of living in cages may have stopped the captive females from releasing pheromones, removing the chemical scent needed to attract wild males.

Article Title: In the 1980s, Scotland planted commercial trees across parts of a 9,000-year-old peatland; decades later, conservationists are removing them to protect wildlife and keep its stored carbon in the groun
Article Text:
A Common Greenshank stood on the edge of a pool of water.

Destruction of a wild habitat

A Common Greenshank stood on the edge of a pool of water.

Reversing the damage at Forsinard Flows

Government backing and broader targets

Bringing communities into the bog

In the 1980s, Scotland planted commercial trees across parts of a 9,000-year-old peatland; decades later, conservationists are removing them to protect wildlife and keep its stored carbon in the ground.The massive project centers on the Flow Country, a vast area of wet bog covering over 400,000 hectares across Caithness and Sutherland in northern Scotland. In July 2024, UNESCO named the area a World Heritage Site, placing it alongside natural treasures like the Great Barrier Reef and the Grand Canyon. It became the world's first peatland to get this special status. King Charles III marked the event by visiting the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) Forsinard Flows reserve to reveal a special plaque.Despite its global fame today, large parts of this ancient landscape were nearly ruined forty years ago. During the 1980s, tax rules and government grants encouraged forestry companies to drain the wet ground, build deer fences, put in roads, and plant long rows of commercial trees.The quick growth of these tree farms hurt the delicate bog. The trees pulled water out of the muddy ground, causing the deep peat soil to dry out and break down.This loss of open land threatened local birds that need wide, treeless spaces to build their nests. Before government action stopped the planting, the region lost about 900 pairs of Golden Plovers, nearly 800 pairs of Dunlins, and 130 pairs of Greenshanks. The area is also a vital home for Hen Harriers, insect-eating sundew plants, Common Scoters, and Red-throated Divers, which lay eggs near small bog pools.Pressure from the Nature Conservancy Council, the RSPB, and other green groups eventually forced the government to change its plans. In January 1988, Malcolm Rifkind, who was then Secretary of State for Scotland, announced that the government would protect over 140,000 hectares of peatland as Sites of Special Scientific Interest. Later that year, Nigel Lawson, then Chancellor, ended the tax breaks and grants that made tree planting on peat profitable.Real cleanup work started in 1994 when the RSPB bought the Forsinard Estate in the middle of the Flow Country, paid for by donations from its members. Today, RSPB Forsinard Flows is the largest nature reserve managed by the charity in the UK.Using money from two big European Union LIFE Nature grants, conservation teams tested ways to cut down the commercial trees, block drainage ditches, and soak the ground again. The main goal is to turn thousands of cleared hectares back into healthy, working bogs.The choice to cut down trees goes beyond helping wildlife. Peatlands are often called the lungs of the Earth because they absorb and trap carbon. The Flow Country alone holds roughly 400 million tonnes of carbon in its soil, which is more carbon than all of the UK’s forests and woods combined. When peat dries out, that trapped carbon leaks back into the air as heat-trapping gas.Peatlands cover over two million hectares across Scotland, making up 25 per cent of the country's land area and more than 60 per cent of all UK peatlands.To help fix this land, the Scottish Government promised £250 million over ten years to restore 250,000 hectares of damaged peatlands by 2030 through its Peatland ACTION Programme. Official records show that over 75,000 hectares have been fixed so far, including a record 10,360 hectares completed during the 2023-24 financial year.Scotland's peatland policy focuses on three main steps: protecting healthy sites, taking care of working land, and fixing damaged areas. New science shows that other practical steps, like keeping farm animals and deer from overgrazing, re-wetting farm soil, and changing how grassy peatlands are used, can cut gas emissions even further.Fixing remote peatlands means working in tough conditions, where cold weather and wet mud make field tasks hard. To gain public and political support, conservation groups built better visitor spots at Forsinard Flows.The reserve now has a lookout tower that offers visitors panoramic views of the surrounding landscape. Recent investments have also added modern research facilities and on-site accommodation, allowing scientists, researchers and volunteers to stay at the reserve while studying how healthy bogs store carbon and support the return of rare bird species.Beside storing carbon and creating homes for wildlife, the Scottish Government sees peatland repair as a way to create green jobs. The long cleanup effort is bringing countryside work to northern Scotland, helping local hotels and cafes, and building up green tourism.
Article Summary: Peatlands cover over two million hectares across Scotland, making up 25 per cent of the country's land area. The Flow Country alone holds roughly 400 million tonnes of carbon in its soil, which is more carbon than all of the UK’s forests and woods combined. When peat dries out, that trapped carbon leaks back into the air as heat-trapping gas.

Article Title: Vietnam moves to bar under-16s from posting, commenting on social media
Article Text:
Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support the idea of requiring social media accounts for children under 16 to be registered through a parent or guardian? Yes, it enhances safety No, it restricts freedom 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Vietnam is planning to require social media platforms to stop users under the age of 16 from posting content, commenting or reacting to posts, under a draft decree aimed at strengthening online protections for children, according to a document reviewed by Reuters.The proposed rules would require social media accounts belonging to children under 16 to be registered using the information of a parent or legal guardian, who would be responsible for supervising the content viewed by children and the amount of time they spend on the platforms.The draft decree also requires social media companies to use technical measures to identify child users and ensure that they receive age-appropriate content. Platforms would have to provide the highest level of privacy protection for child accounts and proactively detect, warn and block access to content related to violence, pornography, gambling, drugs, suicide and other harmful material."The primary objective is not to ban or excessively restrict children's access to social media, but rather to ensure that when children use social media services, they are placed in an age-appropriate environment and protected from inappropriate risks," deputy culture minister Phan Tam said on Thursday during a meeting to discuss the proposed rules.The proposal comes as governments across the world tighten regulations on children's use of social media amid growing concerns over online safety and the impact of harmful content on young users' mental health.Earlier this week, French lawmakers approved a ban on social media access for children under 15. Australia became the first country to impose such a ban, while several other countries are considering similar measures.The draft decree also proposes new restrictions on online gaming by minors. Game operators would be required to verify users' ages, register accounts of children under 16 through a parent or legal guardian, and limit users under 16 to a maximum of 60 minutes of gameplay per day across games offered by the same company.The draft decree has not yet been finalised and may be revised before it is formally adopted.
Article Summary: Vietnam is planning to require social media platforms to stop users under the age of 16 from posting content, commenting or reacting to posts. The draft decree is aimed at strengthening online protections for children. The proposal comes as governments across the world tighten regulations on children's use of social media.

Article Title: Inside Tuvalu: This tiny island nation has just one airline, almost no tourists, and a future threatened by rising seas
Article Text:
Why Tuvalu is considered one of the most vulnerable nations on earth

What NASA's analysis actually found

A rising tide already visible on the ground

Daily life on a shrinking runway between the ocean

A cash economy that only recently modernised

Why a nation this small carries such outsized stakes

Tuvalu is one of the least visited countries on earth. A single airline, Fiji Airways, operates the only scheduled flights in and out, connecting the capital atoll of Funafuti to Fiji a few times a week, and there is no other way to reach the country by air. The entire nation is made up of nine coral atolls covering roughly 26 square kilometres, smaller than many major airports, and is home to just under 11,000 people. Life here has always moved differently from most of the world, shaped by close communal ties and a cash-based economy that only recently saw its first ATMs installed. But scientists now warn Tuvalu faces a far bigger question than isolation: whether the country will remain habitable at all as sea levels continue to rise. Tuvalu's government has also explored more unconventional responses to this crisis, including efforts to digitally preserve the nation's culture and even legal identity, in case rising seas eventually force its population to relocate entirely.Tuvalu's islands sit at an average elevation of only about two metres above sea level, among the lowest of any country on the planet. According to a technical report titled Assessment of Sea Level Rise and Associated Impacts for Tuvalu , produced by NASA 's Sea Level Change Team in support of the United Nations-backed Rising Nations Initiative, Tuvalu has already begun experiencing measurable impacts from the combined effects of rising oceans, storms and natural ocean variability, effects the report expects to worsen in the years ahead.According to NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory , Pacific island nations including Tuvalu, Kiribati and Fiji will experience at least 15 centimetres of sea level rise over the next 30 years, a figure the agency describes as effectively locked in regardless of whether global greenhouse gas emissions change going forward. The analysis was carried out by researchers at the University of Hawaii, working alongside scientists from the University of Colorado and Virginia Tech, at the request of Pacific island governments themselves, and in coordination with the United States Department of State. Nadya Vinogradova Shiffer, who directs ocean physics programs within NASA's Earth Science Division, noted that sea levels will continue rising for centuries, bringing more frequent flooding to coastal communities across the region regardless of near-term emissions decisions.Grace Malie, a youth leader from Tuvalu involved with the Rising Nations Initiative, told NASA that accurate science and data can help her community understand exactly what these sea level projections mean in practice, adding that this information also supports early warning systems the country is actively developing. Malie described the stakes bluntly, saying the future of Tuvalu's young people is already at stake, and that climate change represents a matter of justice and survival rather than simply an environmental concern. NASA researchers noted a genuine shortage of on-the-ground measurement data in Pacific nations like Tuvalu, which is part of why the agency has begun combining satellite-based sea level data with ground station measurements and more detailed land elevation mapping specifically for these vulnerable coastlines.Despite the scale of the threat it faces, Tuvalu remains almost entirely disconnected from global tourism. Fiji Airways is the sole carrier serving the country, and flights operate only a few times each week between Funafuti and Fiji, making Tuvalu one of the hardest countries in the world to simply visit. Funafuti International Airport itself is modest by international standards, a single terminal building sitting so close to the surrounding village that locals can walk directly onto the runway whenever no flight is scheduled.Until quite recently, every transaction in Tuvalu, by locals and visitors alike, had to be conducted entirely in cash, since the country had no ATMs anywhere on its islands. That changed in April 2025, when the National Bank of Tuvalu, the country's only bank, installed the nation's first five ATMs on Funafuti, including machines at Vaiaku village and the airport itself. Prime Minister Feleti Teo described the moment as a significant milestone for the country, while the bank's general manager, Siose Teo, called it a transformative switch that would open doors to broader economic participation for Tuvaluans. Even with this change, banking infrastructure across the country remains extremely limited compared to almost anywhere else in the world.Whatever infrastructure changes come next, the core threat facing Tuvalu remains the same one NASA's sea level science team has been documenting for years: a slow, largely irreversible rise in sea level that threatens not just periodic flooding but the long-term habitability of the country itself. With no natural elevation to retreat to and limited land available for adaptation, Tuvalu has become one of the clearest real-world test cases for what rising seas mean for entire nations, not just coastlines, making its quiet, rarely visited atolls a subject of growing scientific and diplomatic attention far beyond their tiny population and remote location in the middle of the Pacific.
Article Summary: Tuvalu's islands sit at an average elevation of only about two metres above sea level, among the lowest of any country on the planet. Pacific island nations including Tuvalu, Kiribati and Fiji will experience at least 15 centimetres of sea level rise over the next 30 years.

Article Title: How heatwave in Europe is making Europeans understand that why Americans' 'environment choice' makes more sense
Article Text:
Sales surge across the continent



Heat as a public health risk



Cultural mindset changing



Europe’s heatwave has an important lesson for smartphone users across the world



For decades, much of Europe dismissed air conditioning as an unnecessary luxury, whereas Americans embraced it as a standard part of everyday life. But after Western Europe recoded its hottest June on record and another relentless heatwave pushed temperatures above 100°F, Europeans are buying AC units in unprecedented numbers. According to a report by Business Insider, market analysts say the trend is structural, not temporary, signaling a cultural shift toward cooling solutions once seen as wasteful. Residents like Kieron Heath in Essex, England, have changed their minds. After struggling through increasingly hot summers with fans, Heath spent £585 on a portable unit last year. “Once you get one, you realize it was a complete no-brainer,” he told Business Insider. His experience reflects a growing sentiment across Europe: AC is no longer indulgence, but survival.Manufacturers also reported double-digit growth in AC sales across Italy, Spain, France, and Germany. Samsung, Midea, Mitsubishi Electric, and LG all say demand has surged, with some models selling out. Eurovent, the industry’s trade association, expects the momentum to continue, projecting EU household AC units could exceed 100 million by 2030.The shift is driven not just by comfort but by health. EuroMOMO estimated excess deaths across Europe rose from 33,000 in mid-June to more than 45,000 by early July. In England and Wales alone, researchers linked 2,183 deaths to the late June heatwave. “Rising temperatures and more frequent extreme heat events are becoming impossible to ignore,” Eurovent’s Stijn Renneboog said.Europe’s resistance to AC has long been tied to older housing, high electricity costs, and cultural attitudes. Only one in five European households has AC, compared with nine in ten in the U.S. But as heatwaves intensify, Europeans are beginning to understand why Americans see cooling as essential. “The American mindset is, ‘I’m hot, so why would I stay hot?’” Heath said. “Ours has almost been, ‘Well, there is no other choice but to be too hot. ’ That mindset is beginning to change.”In related news, Among other challenges, the deadly heatwave has caused smartphones and other electronic devices to overheat. As a result, many are putting their devices in fridges and freezers to cool them down. But experts say the situation is an important reminder for smartphone users everywhere. According to a report by BBC, Jamie Farnell, who runs Shropshire Phone Repairs, in Wem, said that he was getting “flooded” with repairs of devices with “internal moisture damage”. Farnell believes the damage is a result from smartphones being put in fridges and freezers.“We used to see people putting their phones in rice, which is another common misconception,” he told the publication. “When they get wet you shouldn't put it in rice it doesn't really do anything.”“Now people are seeing these tips where people are putting phones in the fridge or freezer, but it's not safe to do it. If you put it in, there is a risk of moisture that can get in the phone and then when it does dry out the moisture or the condensation turns into water,” Farnell stated before adding that it was an issue he was seeing from customers “both young and old”.
Article Summary: Sales of air conditioning units across Europe have surged. The trend is signaling a cultural shift toward cooling solutions once seen as wasteful. Only one in five European households has AC, compared with nine in ten in the U.S. In England and Wales alone, researchers linked 2,183 deaths to the June heatwave.

Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warns Iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China. Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical"

Article Title: How selling Alaska in 1867 was a costly mistake for Russia
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Why Russia agreed to the Alaska purchase

The hidden wealth Russia gave away

Strategic and geopolitical consequences







In 1867, Russia’s decision to sell Alaska to America turned out to be a historic mistake that was to go unnoticed for years to come. The sum paid by the US was only $7,200,000. Although, in the light of the circumstances at the time, it appeared logical, retrospectively, the act looks extremely shortsighted. Russia found itself economically constrained, geographically far away from the region and fearful of its falling into the hands of the British without any compensation. In reality, however, the region had proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Its vast reserves of oil, gold, and natural resources would later transform it into one of the most economically significant territories in the United States.The choice of selling Alaska was based on economic and political reasons. By the middle of the 19th century, the Russian Empire experienced financial difficulties as a result of the expensive Crimean War. It had become increasingly hard for the country to manage such remote and thinly populated areas as Alaska.According to EBSCO , “the Russian-American Company was in decline, and the colony failed to yield any profit”.In addition to this, the lucrative fur trade had declined, making the territory much less economically valuable for the empire.At the same time, Russia was afraid that Britain might capture Alaska in case another war broke out between the two countries. Selling the colony to the friendly United States appeared as a logical step. As the Office of the Historian states, William H. Seward, U.S. Secretary of State, “it was a chance to expand its influence in North America and hinder further growth of Britain”.For Russia, the transaction was a chance to minimise the losses. However, it greatly undervalued the potential of Alaska.Another thing that Russia did not expect was the amount of riches that Alaska possessed. Within several decades after the acquisition, the state saw discoveries of enormous deposits of gold, oil, and other minerals.“Alaska has produced more than 40 million ounces of gold,” according to the US Geological Survey. Furthermore, Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) . But even more importantly, the state's oil deposits turned out to be extremely valuable. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968 and became one of North America's biggest.In retrospect, the amount paid by the Americans, $7.2 million, or two cents per acre, was rather laughable. According to Howard I. Kushner , the deal “robbed Russia of an enormously rich territory, the true value of which would only be recognised in the twentieth century.”In addition to resources, there is the question of strategy and how important Alaska is to the United States from a strategic standpoint. This is a very good place when it comes to defence strategy. It borders on the Arctic Ocean and also happens to be close to Russia.During the period of the Cold War, the Alaskan region became a frontier area for the United States, becoming home to military facilities and warning systems.According to Col. Michael J. Forsyth, U.S. Army, the closeness of Russia and Alaska, only about ninety kilometres apart across the Bering Strait, meant that this region became highly significant to the United States' defence plans.From today's point of view, the strategic location of Alaska makes the state very important to the policies of the U.S. related to the Arctic, energy security, and even environmental policies.Thinking back, what seems clear to us now is that the Russians sold Alaska due to immediate needs rather than future considerations. In order to solve the problem, they lost a valuable resource for Russia.Conclusively, the Alaska Purchase should not have been done as it has had a significant impact that will remain throughout history.
Article Summary: Russia sold Alaska to the U.S. in 1867 for only $7,200,000. The sale was based on economic and political reasons. However, the region proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies





AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.

Article Title: '51 wounds, cold-blooded murder': Prosecution seeks death penalty for ex-AAP neta Tahir Hussain, 4 others in IB officer's murder
Article Text:
IB staffer murder case: Prosecution seeks death sentence for Tahir Hussain, other convicts





New Delhi: The prosecution Monday sought death penalty against former AAP councillor Tahir Hussain and four others convicted of the murder of Intelligence Bureau officer Ankit Sharma during the 2020 northeast Delhi riots.The court of additional sessions judge Parveen Singh was hearing the matter concerning Hussain, Nazim, Kasim, Javed and Anas, who were convicted on July 13.Special public prosecutor Madhukar Pandey argued in the court that the murder was "exceptionally brutal"."Ankit Sharma was abducted and relentlessly assaulted before he was killed. A total of 51 wounds were found on his body, 18 of these were inflicted with sharp weapons. The nature of the weapons used shows the intent and diabolical nature of the crime. They fell to the level of being animals. Even after the victim died, they kept on the assault," he said.Calling it a "cold-blooded murder", Pandey added, "These people turned into butchers during the crime. There was not even a single cloth except underwear on the body of Sharma. These people should be kept behind bars, (and) given the maximum death sentence."Opposing the state's plea, Hussain's counsel, advocates Rajiv Mohan and Tara Narula, argued that no specific role had been attributed to their client and that six of the 11 accused had been acquitted in the case.Mohan submitted that the death penalty is warranted only in the "rarest of rare cases", adding that "the punishment of death cannot be determined merely on the basis of the injuries sustained. His (Hussain) conduct was good in jail during the custody."Referring to Hussain's acquittal under Section 120B (criminal conspiracy) of the erstwhile Indian Penal Code, the defence further argued, "Police themselves were unable to control the violent mob, and in such a situation, a single individual cannot be held responsible for the murder. He should be given a chance to reform."Hussain was earlier convicted of murder, kidnapping or abduction with intent to secretly and wrongfully confine a person, rioting and unlawful assembly, promoting enmity between groups, and disobedience of a public servant's order under erstwhile IPC.
Article Summary: Tahir Hussain, Nazim, Kasim, Javed and Anas convicted of murder of Ankit Sharma. Sharma was abducted and relentlessly assaulted before he was killed. Hussain's counsel argued that no specific role had been attributed to their client.

Article Title: Delhi weather: Rain brings relief from humidity, IMD forecasts more showers over next few days
Article Text:
Delhi's morning rain has alleviated the burdensome humidity, as per the India Meteorological Department's latest updates





NEW DELHI: Delhi woke up to showers on Tuesday as rain lashed several parts of the national capital, offering some relief from humid conditions, while the India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecast more rainfall over the next few days.The weather department has forecast a generally cloudy sky with one or two spells of very light to light rain at most places and moderate rain at a few places from morning to noon.Another spell of rain is likely towards the evening or night.The IMD has forecast moderate rainfall over Delhi on Wednesday, with light to moderate rain likely at several places during the day.According to the IMD's daily weather report issued on Monday, the national capital is likely to witness light rain and thunderstorms over the next few days, with generally cloudy skies and moderate rain at isolated places.Delhi recorded a maximum temperature of 38.1 degrees Celsius and a minimum temperature of 28.6 degrees Celsius at Safdarjung.The IMD said maximum temperatures are likely to fall by 2-3 degrees Celsius over the next six days.According to the IMD, the deep depression was located near the West Bengal coast and was likely to move nearly west-northwestwards and cross the West Bengal-North Odisha coasts near Digha and west of Haldia by early Tuesday morning.The weather system was located close to Digha in West Bengal, with its movement likely to bring rain to several parts of the region.The IMD has advised commuters to check traffic conditions before leaving and avoid areas prone to waterlogging.(With ANI inputs)
Article Summary: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast more rainfall over the next few days. The weather system was located close to Digha in West Bengal, with its movement likely to bring rain to several parts of the region. The IMD has advised commuters to check traffic conditions before leaving and avoid areas prone to waterlogging.

Article Title: Sports journalist Jasvinder Sidhu dies after being hit by bike in east Delhi
Article Text:
Sidhu had gone to visit a fellow journalist who had been admitted to a Patparganj hospital after suffering a brain haemorrhage.





NEW DELHI: A sports journalist died after being hit by a motorcycle while he was crossing a road on NH-9 in east Delhi ’s Ghazipur early Monday. The bike rider, who travelling from the Meerut side, also sustained injuries and is in a serious condition.The deceased, Jasvinder Sidhu, was a resident of Kalkaji. The rider, Asif (35), is a resident of Khatauli in UP’s Muzaffarnagar district.Police received a PCR call about the accident at 12.16 am. Sidhu was taken to LBS Hospital and later referred to GTB Hospital, where doctors declared him brought dead.Sidhu had gone to visit a fellow journalist who had been admitted to a Patparganj hospital after suffering a brain haemorrhage. It was while he was returning that he was hit by the motorcycle.Police registered a case under BNS sections 281 (rash driving or riding on a public way) and 106(1) (causing death by negligence). Investigators suspect the motorcycle was being ridden at high speed and that the rider lost control.A fellow journalist said he was unsure why Sidhu had gone onto the highway. “The impact flung him into the air. It appears he was dragged for some distance, as most of his clothes were torn.”“The ambulance arrived within about 20 minutes and shifted both Sidhu and the injured motorcyclist to the hospital. Sidhu was conscious when we reached the hospital. He gave me the password to his mobile phone and told me his father’s name. After that, he went into shock. The doctors performed CPR and other emergency procedures, and he briefly revived,” the journalist recalled.“He had multiple fractures and severe abrasions all over his body. His clothes were almost completely torn off due to the impact,” the journalist said.Sidhu had been a journalist for more than two decades and was well known for covering sports in prominent newspapers, he added.Sidhu’s sister Inderjeet Bhatia said he was unmarried. Their elder brother died in 2010-11 due to a prolonged illness.“He was always willing to help others. Whenever anyone was in trouble or going through a difficult time, he would be the first person to stand by them after just one phone call.” His friends remembered him as “a gem of a person”, an accomplished writer and a sharp analyst.“We are deeply saddened by the untimely demise of veteran sports journalist Jaswinder Sidhu in a tragic road accident . A familiar and respected presence at Press Club, his passing marks a profound loss to Indian journalism. His dedication to sports journalism, unwavering professionalism and insightful reporting earned him immense respect across the media fraternity,” Press Club of India posted on X.
Article Summary: Jasvinder Sidhu had gone to visit a fellow journalist who had been admitted to a Patparganj hospital. It was while he was returning that he was hit by the motorcycle. The bike rider, who travelling from the Meerut side, also sustained injuries and is in a serious condition.

Article Title: Credit card trail exposes online jewellery fraud
Article Text:
New Delhi:





A woman’s attempt to buy jewellery through a social media advertisement turned into a cyber fraud, but a digital and financial investigation led police to the accused’s doorstep in Haryana According to police, the complainant came across an advertisement for jewellery on social media in Feb and tried calling the number mentioned in the post. Though the call did not connect, she soon received a callback from another number.The caller, posing as a representative of the jewellery seller, shifted the conversation to another platform and allegedly convinced her to transfer money on the assurance that the jewellery would be delivered. However, the promised products never arrived.Police claimed the woman lost nearly Rs 1.2 lakh through multiple UPI transactions before realising she had been cheated. Based on her complaint, an FIR was registered at the cyber police station of central district under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.“During the investigation, our team analysed the social media account, digital footprints and financial transactions linked to the fraud,” said DCP (central) Rohit Rajbir Singh.“They found that most of the cheated amount had not been routed through conventional bank accounts but was instead used to clear outstanding dues on two credit cards.”Police said Rs 97,580 was settled against one credit card and the remaining Rs 19,395 against another, a strategy allegedly adopted to obscure the money trail.The investigation eventually led the cops to Hodal in Haryana’s Palwal district, where they arrested Ankit Thakur, 26. During interrogation, he allegedly disclosed that he used a SIM card linked to one of the credit cards to receive OTPs and facilitate fraudulent transactions.Police said he admitted to sharing the proceeds with his associate who is absconding. A mobile phone and an active SIM allegedly used in the offence have been seized.
Article Summary: Police claim the woman lost nearly Rs 1.2 lakh through multiple UPI transactions. The investigation eventually led the cops to Hodal in Haryana’s Palwal district. Ankit Thakur, 26, allegedly used a SIM card linked to one of the credit cards to receive OTPs and facilitate fraudulent transactions.

Article Title: SevenHills proposal back for approval, as BMC moves to revive hospital under new promoter
Article Text:
SevenHills hospital revival plan promises 300 beds for BMC patients





Richa PintoMumbai: Nearly two months after the BMC Improvement Committee sent back a proposal seeking to hand over the sprawling SevenHills Hospital campus at Marol to Capri Global Ventures Pvt Ltd, the civic administration has returned with the proposal. The Shiv Sena (UBT) and Congress had opposed the proposal and questioned the timing, transparency and terms of the move. The proposal was not rejected, but was returned to the administration for reconsideration following a heated discussion in the committee meeting.Capri Global, which emerged as the successful resolution applicant for SevenHills Healthcare Pvt Ltd (SHPL) under the insolvency process, will receive equity-based support from Reliance Foundation, which manages H N Reliance Hospital in Girgaum.The proposal authorises the execution of a fresh lease deed with SHPL, now under Capri Global’s ownership, allowing the hospital to continue under the original public-private partnership (PPP) model. It provides for a 30-year lease, extendable by another 30 years, for nearly 66,688 sq m of BMC land at Marol, Andheri (East), where the hospital is located.The SevenHills Hospital project was awarded in 2004 under a PPP model, with the concessionaire required to construct and operate a 1,300-bed hospital while reserving 20% of beds and OPD services for BMC-referred patients.However, only 306 beds became operational. In 2018, the BMC issued a show-cause notice for terminating the agreement, alleging the concessionaire had defaulted on ₹140.88 crore in lease rent and property tax and had failed to provide the agreed services to civic patients.The dispute subsequently went through insolvency proceedings before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) and the Supreme Court. Capri Global later emerged as the successful resolution applicant, with the NCLT approving its resolution plan, making it the new shareholder of SHPL.Under the approved resolution plan, SevenHills Hospital will be redeveloped as a 1,500-bed not-for-profit tertiary care hospital. The new promoter has agreed to honour the conditions of the original 2005 contract and the 2013 memorandum of understanding, including reserving 20% of operational beds—300 beds—and 20% of OPD services for BMC patients, with treatment, medicines and diagnostic tests provided at civic rates.The proposal also states that the original PPP agreement and memorandum of understanding were never formally terminated. “Consequently, the civic body will execute a fresh lease deed reflecting the revised ownership structure so that it can be placed before the NCLT and other judicial forums, wherever required,” states the proposal.Civic officials said the revival of SevenHills Hospital is expected to significantly augment Mumbai’s public healthcare infrastructure by bringing a long-defunct mega hospital back into operation while preserving the quota of subsidised treatment for BMC patients under the PPP model.
Article Summary: The proposal was not rejected, but was returned to the administration for reconsideration. The Shiv Sena (UBT) and Congress had opposed the proposal and questioned the timing, transparency and terms of the move. Capri Global emerged as the successful resolution applicant for SevenHills Healthcare Pvt Ltd (SHPL) under the insolvency process.

Article Title: BMC seeks nod for Rs 14.5cr contract for river trash traps
Article Text:
The previous maintenance contract lapsed on Sept 30, 2025

Mumbai:





BMC has sought approval to award a two-year contract for Rs 14.5-crore for operation and maintenance of trash boom systems installed across six rivers and nullahs near mangrove belts in the city’s western suburbs to prevent floating waste from entering Arabian Sea.The proposal, which will come up before the civic standing committee on Thursday.BMC installed the systems in July 2022 following directions from National Green Tribunal (NGT) to prevent plastic waste from flowing through rivers and drains into mangrove ecosystems and the sea. The trapped waste is removed and scientifically disposed of.The previous maintenance contract lapsed on Sept 30, 2025. BMC continued operations till Feb by utilising the 4% contingency provision under the contract.Following a tendering process, Virgo Specialties Pvt Ltd emerged as the lowest bidder after negotiations, quoting 1.3% below BMC’s estimate.Until the new contract receives approval, the civic administration has sought permission to continue the work under the BMC chief’s emergency powers.
Article Summary: BMC has sought approval to award a two-year contract for Rs 14.5-crore for operation and maintenance of trash boom systems. The previous maintenance contract lapsed on Sept 30, 2025. Virgo Specialties Pvt Ltd emerged as the lowest bidder after negotiations.
